quick: Use only if clearly needed; topical preferred
Limited data; brief topical use likely low risk
Limit duration to avoid rebound congestion
summary: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-adrenergic agonist used as a nasal decongestant for temporary relief of congestion from colds, allergies and sinusitis. The 0.05% nasal spray is dosed 2-3 sprays per nostril every 10-12 hours and must not be used for more than 3 consecutive days to avoid rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). Ophthalmic and dermatologic (rosacea) formulations also exist.
indications: Temporary relief of nasal congestion due to common cold, hay fever or other upper respiratory allergies
Temporary relief of sinus congestion and pressure
Ophthalmic 0.025%: temporary relief of redness of the eye due to minor irritation (OTC)
Topical 1% cream (Rx): persistent facial erythema of rosacea in adults

dosage.c: Nasal congestion, adults and children >=6 yr (0.05%)
dosage.t: Not more often than every 10-12 hours
dosage.n: Do not exceed 2 doses in 24 h; do not use >3 days
Use only under direction; do not use >3 days
Do not use longer than 72 hours

admin: Spray into each nostril without tilting the head back; sniff gently
Do not use more often than every 10-12 hours and not more than twice in 24 hours
Do not use the nasal product for more than 3 days to avoid rebound congestion
Wipe the nozzle clean after use; do not share the container to prevent spread of infection
For eye drops, do not touch the dropper tip to the eye
moa: Oxymetazoline is a direct-acting sympathomimetic with predominant alpha-adrenergic (alpha-1 and alpha-2) agonist activity. Local application constricts dilated arterioles in nasal or conjunctival mucosa, reducing blood flow, mucosal swelling and congestion, thereby decreasing tissue hyperemia and edema.

absolute: Concurrent or recent (within 14 days) MAO inhibitor use (per general sympathomimetic precaution)
relative: Heart disease, hypertension, thyroid disease, diabetes
Difficulty urinating due to enlarged prostate

preg: Topical use is generally preferred over systemic decongestants. Use only if clearly needed and after consulting a clinician; limited human data. Avoid excessive or prolonged use.
lact: Limited data on excretion into breast milk; brief topical use is likely associated with low infant exposure. Consult a clinician before use during breastfeeding.
renal: No dose adjustment required for short-term topical use given minimal systemic absorption.
hepatic: No dose adjustment required for short-term topical use given minimal systemic absorption.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) - risk of hypertensive reaction with systemic sympathomimetics; avoid within 14 days
moderate: Tricyclic antidepressants - may potentiate pressor effects
Other sympathomimetics / decongestants - additive cardiovascular effects
Beta-blockers - possible unopposed alpha effect with significant systemic absorption
minor: Antihypertensive agents - theoretical reduced effect if systemically absorbed
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction for topical use.

common: Local nasal burning, stinging, dryness or sneezing
serious: Rebound nasal congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) with prolonged use
Hypertension or palpitations with excessive systemic absorption
rare: Bradycardia and CNS depression (especially in young children after ingestion)
emergency: Accidental ingestion in children causing coma, bradycardia and respiratory depression

monitoring: Duration of nasal use (limit to 3 days)
Blood pressure/heart rate in patients with cardiovascular disease if used repeatedly
counsel: Do not use the nasal spray for more than 3 days in a row
Use of more than directed may cause burning, sneezing or worsening (rebound) congestion
Keep out of reach of children; accidental swallowing can be dangerous in young children
Temporary stinging or sneezing may occur
Stop and consult a clinician if symptoms persist or worsen
pk: Store at room temperature; do not freeze
pearls: Long-acting decongestant (10-12 h) versus phenylephrine - but limit to 3 days to prevent rhinitis medicamentosa
Pediatric ingestion is a recognized poisoning emergency (CNS depression, bradycardia) - keep away from children
Topical 1% cream (Rx) is an FDA-approved treatment for persistent facial erythema of rosacea
Brimonidine and oxymetazoline are the two approved topical alpha-agonists for rosacea redness
missed: This medicine is used as needed for symptom relief, so there is no fixed missed-dose schedule. Do not use more frequently than every 10-12 hours and do not exceed the labeled maximum to make up for missed use.
overdose: Topical overuse can cause rebound congestion and systemic sympathomimetic effects. Accidental ingestion, particularly in children, can cause sedation, bradycardia, hypotension/hypertension and respiratory depression; this is a medical emergency. Treatment is supportive; contact a poison control center.
